title: In great-ape lineages, small deletions and substitutions avoid non-conserved human regulatory DNA to a similar small degree after composition matching; CTCF-only elements resist deletions more
abstract: In the chimpanzee, gorilla and orangutan lineages, human regulatory DNA that is not conserved across mammals lost bases to small deletions and to substitutions at similar small rates below background once local sequence composition was matched, so we find no general function in this DNA that depends on its length or presence rather than its sequence; CTCF-only elements are the exception. This matters because tests for hidden function in such dark DNA usually use point mutations, which cannot see a function that tolerates base changes but needs the DNA to be present; deletions test this directly, and fixed ape differences record selection over 6-15 million years. From alignments of the human genome (hg38) to four primate assemblies we found 3.92 million lineage-specific deletions and 62.7 million substitutions. We compared ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs: regions with chromatin marks of regulation) in which at most 5% of bases are conserved across 241 mammals (Zoonomia phyloP >= 2.27) with matched background DNA (stratified Mantel-Haenszel rate ratios; 5-Mb block bootstrap). The deficit is 1 minus the rate ratio. The key test compares 1-10 bp deletions with substitutions at the same bases, outside repeats and more than 11 bp from any conserved base, with strata for region, GC, gene distance, short repeats, local conservation and fine-scale composition. The deletion deficit exceeded the substitution deficit by 2.1 points (95% CI 1.2 to 2.9) in these cCREs, by -1.8 in cCREs with no conserved base, by -2.4 at non-conserved bases of conserved cCREs, by -2.0 in flank DNA and by 45 in coding sequence (frameshifts). CTCF-only elements kept an excess of 8.0 points (5.8 to 10.0; 6.4 to 10.0 in single lineages). Without composition strata the excess in all non-conserved cCREs was 6.8 points; it came mostly from AT-rich sequence. Overall deficits are small (deletions 2-13%, substitutions 2-6%) against 42% and 69% for conserved non-coding DNA, and in transposon-derived cCRE DNA repeat-specific deletion processes dominate. Large deletions (101-20,000 bp) avoided these cCREs per base at 2-3.5% of the level of a conserved base. Limits: a systematic floor of about 2-5 points; the CTCF excess could also reflect raised substitution mutation at CTCF sites; cCRE activity is measured in human cells. Two independent reviews changed the analysis and the conclusion.

(b) Deletion deficit minus substitution deficit at the same bases (outside repeats, more than 11 bp from any mammal-conserved base), with the main strata (light) and with four extra local-composition strata (dark): after composition control, bulk non-conserved cCREs show at most about 2 points, CTCF-only elements about 8.

citations.reason: Human gnomAD-SV deletions found non-conserved cCRE DNA much less constrained than conserved DNA; fixed ape deletions give small deletion deficits of the same order as substitution deficits.

Human rare-variant excess in cCREs without conserved bases is 2-7% of conserved DNA; our ape substitution constraint and conserved-equivalent size (about 30 Mb) agree, and deletions add at most a few points.
